title: A Jet Blew Up 10 km Up. One Flight Attendant Fell the Whole Way, and Lived
description:
Case 005, the full case file. On 26 January 1972, JAT Flight 367, a DC-9 flying from Stockholm to Belgrade, took off from Copenhagen at 3:15 pm with 28 people on board. At 4:01 pm, 10,160 metres over Czechoslovakia, a bomb in the forward baggage compartment tore it apart. Flight attendant Vesna Vulović, 22, who by her own account was only on the flight because the airline confused her with another attendant called Vesna, was the only survivor. She was pinned inside a section of the fuselage by a food trolley; the wreckage came down at an angle on a snowy, wooded hillside near Srbská Kamenice, where villager Bruno Honke, a former wartime medic, heard her and kept her alive until rescuers arrived. Her doctors later said her low blood pressure made her pass out quickly and kept her heart from bursting on impact. She had a fractured skull, three broken vertebrae and two broken legs, and was temporarily paralysed from the waist down; within ten months she was walking again. JAT gave her a desk job negotiating freight contracts. In 1985 Paul McCartney presented her with her Guinness World Records Hall of Fame award for the highest fall survived without a parachute. No one was ever arrested for the bombing. In 2009 two journalists argued the aircraft had been shot down at a much lower altitude; the Czech aviation authority dismissed the claim and the record still stands. Vesna Vulović died in Belgrade in December 2016, aged 66. Rook didn't believe it either.

In memory of the 27 passengers and crew who died.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. Scenes, sets and all of Rook's actions are dramatised; nobody's words are quoted.

source_notes: LONG-FORM ADDITIONS (checked on 13 Nov 2026). How it was checked: this run could not open web pages directly (the session's network only allowed web search), so every added fact was checked against search-result extracts of the pages listed in 'sources' and against the notes the Short's run made from the full pages. Nothing was added that did not appear in at least two of them, except where marked. 1971 and the Beatles: Guinness says she and her friends grew up listening to the Beatles; Lincoln Parish Journal says that in 1971 the 21-year-old met a friend who was an air hostess and then applied to JAT; Wikipedia has the same friend-in-uniform story. That the meeting happened on a Belgrade street, the record shop and the dancing are dramatised. Coffee: Wikipedia reports her own account that she knew her low blood pressure would fail her at the medical and drank a large amount of coffee before it; a second, weaker source (migflug) says she hid her low blood pressure from the examiners. The script says 'by her own account'. Timeline: left Copenhagen at 3:15 pm, explosion at 4:01 pm, 46 minutes later (Wikipedia JAT Flight 367, Aviation Safety Network); 28 people on board, 27 killed; DC-9-32 Stockholm-Copenhagen-Zagreb-Belgrade; her crew boarded in Copenhagen. Bomb: a briefcase bomb in the forward baggage compartment (Czechoslovak investigation, per Wikipedia and Guinness). Claim: the next day a man describing himself as a Croatian nationalist telephoned the Swedish newspaper Kvällsposten and claimed responsibility; no arrests were ever made (Wikipedia JAT Flight 367, TWZ). The script reports the call and that nobody was arrested; it does not say who did it. Why she lived: investigators credited the food cart that pinned her inside the fuselage section and the angle and snow of the landing; her physicians said her low blood pressure made her pass out quickly when the cabin depressurised and kept her heart from bursting on impact (Wikipedia; Deseret News: doctors 'attributed her survival to low blood pressure'). Injuries: fractured skull, three broken vertebrae, two broken legs (Guinness); temporarily paralysed from the waist down (Wikipedia). Coma length differs by source (days, ten days, 27 days), so the script only says she was in a coma. First request on waking, a cigarette: Wikipedia and View from the Wing (citing obituaries). Memory: she never recalled the explosion or the fall (all sources). Flight home: treated in Prague until 12 March 1972, then flown to Belgrade; she declined an injection to make her sleep on the flight because she had no memory of the crash to fear (Wikipedia). Walking within ten months, lifelong limp (Guinness, Wikipedia). Desk job negotiating freight contracts after she asked to return to work (Wikipedia, Montreal Gazette obituary). 1985: Paul McCartney presented her certificate and medal at the Guinness Hall of Fame ceremony (Guinness). The city of the ceremony was not confirmed in this run, so it is not named; the presenter on stage is a generic figure in a dark suit, not a likeness. Dismissal: sources say 1990 or 'the early 1990s', for speaking and protesting against Slobodan Milošević (View from the Wing citing the BBC obituary; Wikipedia); the script says 'the early nineties'. Death: December 2016 in Belgrade, aged 66 (Armenpress, Inquirer/AP, Wikipedia). 2009 dispute: as in the Short's notes below. The graphic's 'about 800 m' is the claim's figure. Dramatised in the long form, not reported: the look of every set (street, clinic, crew office, newspaper desk, stage, ward), the wall gauge, the cups, the flight tag on the rota, the crew walking out in Copenhagen, the clock, the stretcher party, the doctor at the bed, the toes under the blanket, Rook's fear on the flight home, the jet in the office window, the empty chair, and everything Rook does. No dialogue is attributed to anyone; on-screen words are labels. The victims are not shown. FROM THE SHORT: Date, flight and aircraft: 26 January 1972, JAT Flight 367, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9 flying Stockholm to Belgrade with stops in Copenhagen and Zagreb; Vulović and her crew boarded in Copenhagen (Guinness World Records, Wikipedia, The War Zone). Cause: investigators attributed the explosion to a briefcase bomb in the baggage compartment (Guinness, Wikipedia; The War Zone says 'luggage hold'); Croatian nationalists were blamed and no one was ever arrested (all three). The script says only 'a bomb in the baggage hold' and names no group; the place (the aircraft broke up over Srbská Kamenice, Czechoslovakia) is given in the on-screen labels. Deaths: Wikipedia says she was 'the only survivor of the 28 passengers and crew', The War Zone 'all 27 other passengers and crew'; the script says twenty-seven people were killed. Height: 10,160 m / 33,330 ft (Wikipedia, The War Zone), 33,333 ft (Guinness); the script rounds to 'ten kilometres' and 'ten thousand metres' and the graphics show 10,160 m. Mix-up: the airline 'confused her for another flight attendant also named Vesna' (Wikipedia; Guinness and The War Zone agree). Trolley: 'pinned down by a food cart' (Guinness), 'trapped by a food trolley in the DC-9's fuselage' (Wikipedia). Sources disagree on whether she was in the tail or the middle of the aircraft (she herself said the middle), so the script says 'inside the wreckage' and the animation shows a length of fuselage with no tail. Landing: the fuselage 'landed at an angle in a heavily wooded and snow-covered mountainside' (Wikipedia; Guinness: thick snow 'at a favourable angle'). Rescue: villager Bruno Honke 'heard her screaming amid the wreckage'; he had been a medic in the Second World War and kept her alive until rescuers arrived (Wikipedia, Guinness). The War Zone calls the rescuer an unnamed woodsman who heard her cries in the dark. Injuries: fractured skull, two broken legs, three broken vertebrae (Guinness); Wikipedia adds broken ribs and pelvis; the script says 'broken skull, broken legs, broken spine'. Recovery: able to walk again 'after ten months' (Guinness), 'within ten months' (Wikipedia); she was temporarily paralysed from the waist down and limped for the rest of her life. Coma length is given as three, ten or 27 days depending on the source, so the script does not mention it. Dispute: in 2009 two Prague-based journalists claimed the aircraft was shot down by mistake at about 800 m; the Czech Civil Aviation Authority dismissed this, the journalists called their own evidence circumstantial, and Guinness World Records continues to list the record (Wikipedia, Guinness). The script says 'some reporters later doubted the height. The record still stands.' Her age (22) follows from the birth date 3 January 1950 on Wikipedia; Guinness says 23; the age is only in the description. Dramatised, not reported: the crew roster graphic (the other attendant is shown only as 'Vesna' with her surname blacked out, because this run did not verify it, and the sliding flight tag is an illustration of the mix-up), the dial altimeter, the exact look of the aircraft, cabin, stairs, hillside, village and hospital ward, the lantern, Vulović pushing the trolley at the moment of the explosion (she had no memory of the flight), the X-ray graphic, the newspaper, and everything Rook does. No dialogue is attributed to anyone. The victims are not shown after the explosion.
